---
title: "Step 5 — Do the reading"
subtitle: "Step 5 of 5"
---

**Time:** 25 minutes.
**Before you start:** nothing. Do this on the train.
**When you finish:** you have read one short paper and written 3 sentences about
it.

This is the last step. It is short, and it feeds the critical appraisal session
later in the week.

## Step 1 of 2 — Read one paper

1. Choose one paper from the list below, or use one of your own.
2. Read the abstract, the methods and the first table. Skip the discussion.

**You should see:** a study design you can name, and a measure of association
you can find in the text.

**If it does not work:** if you cannot tell which design it is, that is a useful
finding. Bring the paper and we will work it out together.

| Paper | Why this one |
|---|---|
| Doll R, Hill AB. Smoking and carcinoma of the lung. *BMJ* 1950;2:739–48. [Open](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.2.4682.739) | The case-control study that started modern epidemiology. Short, readable, and the reasoning is all on the surface. |
| Snow J. On the mode of communication of cholera. 1855. [Open](https://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/snow/snowbook.html) | Read only the Broad Street section. Natural experiment, done with no statistics at all. |
| A recent paper from your own field | The one you will actually argue about. |

## Step 2 of 2 — Write 3 sentences

Write these down. Bring them on paper or on your laptop.

1. What design is this study, and how do you know?
2. What measure of association does it report, and what is its value?
3. Name one thing other than the exposure that could explain the result.

**You should see:** 3 short sentences. A few lines each is enough.

**If it does not work:** if you cannot answer question 3, look at who was
recruited and how the exposure was measured. [Primer
9](primer-epi-04-bias.qmd) covers both.

## Optional background reading

Read these only if you have time. None of them is assumed on the first day.

| Topic | Source |
|---|---|
| Study designs, in one page each | Grimes DA, Schulz KF. An overview of clinical research: the lay of the land. *Lancet* 2002;359:57–61. |
| Bias, plainly explained | Delgado-Rodríguez M, Llorca J. Bias. *J Epidemiol Community Health* 2004;58:635–41. |
| Why absolute risks matter | Gigerenzer G et al. Helping doctors and patients make sense of health statistics. *Psychol Sci Public Interest* 2007;8:53–96. |
| R, if you want more than the primers | Wickham H, Çetinkaya-Rundel M, Grolemund G. *R for Data Science*, 2nd edition. [Free online](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) |

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this matters
One session later in the week is a critical appraisal exercise in groups. It
works only if everybody arrives having read at least one paper closely enough to
argue about it.

The 3 questions are the same 3 we ask of every paper on the course.
:::

## You have finished the prelude

All 5 steps are done. Your laptop works, you have run R, and you have read a
paper closely enough to argue about it.

See you at IISc on Monday 21 September.

The programme will be circulated separately.
